value.text: Home Schools InnovatED Phase 2 town hall set for Monday at Sebastian River Middle by Tina Hodges Nov 15, 2026 / 12:23 PM A A A A Reset InnovatED (School District of IRC) Share on Twitter Share via Email SEBASTIAN — The School District of Indian River County will hold an InnovatED Phase 2 town hall Monday, November 16, from 5:30 to 6:30 p.m. at Sebastian River Middle School to gather public feedback on two facility proposals still under consideration. District officials have invited families, staff, and community members to hear details, ask questions, and share thoughts on the plans. The two proposals focus on a future home for Wabasso School that would add capacity and specialized learning spaces, and on creating a connected arts pathway in Sebastian. Both remain under review, with School Board consideration expected in December. Wabasso School currently serves students with specialized needs on U.S. District leaders have previously described the campus as at capacity and have discussed relocating the program to the former Glendale Elementary site in Vero Beach to allow room for growth and more tailored spaces for life skills and independent learning. The arts pathway proposal involves Sebastian Elementary School of the Arts, which officials have said could share the Sebastian River Middle School campus as a separate school while maintaining its own identity. This is the latest in a series of InnovatED community sessions. Phase 1 of the initiative, which included several school relocations, shared campuses, and boundary adjustments, took effect for the 2026-27 school year after School Board approval in December 2025. The original Sebastian River Middle School town hall for Phase 2 was postponed from Nov. Residents who cannot attend can still submit questions or comments. Share input with the planning team. The meeting is open to the public. Sebastian Daily is the number-one source for local news with more readers than any other publication in Sebastian, Vero Beach, Fellsmere, and Indian River County. The 37th Stuart Air Show brought aviation fans young and old together for a picture-perfect weekend filled with aircraft, family traditions, and appreciation for veterans.Organizers said the weekend got off to a strong start Friday night with a drone and fireworks show and continued with large crowds throughout the weekend."Stuart Air Show has had an amazing weekend Friday night with our drone and fireworks show. We had a great turnout," Chrissy Valvano said. "Sunday, we're looking at a record turnout for Veterans Appreciation Day, and this weather could not be better."For some families, attending the Stuart Air Show has become a tradition passed down through the years."The Stuart Air Show has been a part of our community for many years," Sarah Naylor said. "We have many memories of coming in the past, as long as I can remember."For younger aviation fans Wyatt and Ivy Rotan, some of the biggest attractions were the military aircraft."I like coming to the Stuart Air Show because I like to see the C-17 and the F-16 fly," Wyatt said."I like seeing the C-17," Ivy added.The event also gave young people a chance to learn more about aviation while honoring those who served."You get to have a lot of fun around here, just going around and seeing a bunch of planes," John Gefell said. "Also, because I'm working on my aviation merit badge as a Boy Scout and my grandpa was a veteran, so it’s just real fun to come out here and just have a lot of fun."With beautiful weather and a strong turnout, the 37th Stuart Air Show once again brought the community together, giving longtime fans and a new generation of aviation enthusiasts a weekend to remember.

Thousands of people dressed in red filled downtown West Palm Beach for this year’s American Heart Association Heart Walk, taking steps to support a cause that touches many families across the community.About 3,000 people took part in the event, which brings together survivors, families and supporters to raise awareness about heart disease and stroke.WATCH: 3,000 walkers fill downtown West Palm Beach for Heart WalkWPTV is a proud sponsor of the Heart Walk, and WPTV’s Ashley Glass served as emcee for this year’s event.For some of the families walking, the mission is deeply personal.WPTV’s Christy Waite has been connecting with the family of a young girl named Blake, whose health journey has included heart failure and multiple open-heart surgeries.Before Blake was born, her parents learned she had a heart condition that would lead to multiple heart surgeries. When Blake was just 14 months old, she became very sick."She was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes, and that put her heart into heart failure, so she had to have open-heart surgery as soon as possible," her mom, Devin Aubrey, said.Unfortunately, the surgery didn't work, and a few months later Blake had her second open-heart surgery. Doctors put in a mechanical valve to help her heart open and close.As Blake continues to grow, so does her heart, but not the valve. When she is a little older, she will need to have another surgery to fix it.Blake's family formed Team Blake to give back and raise money through the Heart Walk.This year, Team Blake raised $10,000, surpassing the amount the team raised last year.Team Blake wasn’t the only one celebrating a fundraising milestone.This year’s Heart Walk raised more than $1.4 million, setting a new fundraising record.For the walkers who filled downtown West Palm Beach, each step represented a different story, from survivors celebrating how far they’ve come to families walking in support of someone they love.

Trump International Airport continued to face flight cancellations and delays Saturday, a day after the Federal Aviation Administration lifted a nationwide ground stop that disrupted air travel across the country.WATCH: Travelers Stranded as FAA Ground Stop Fallout ContinuesThe FAA's air traffic control system was back at full operations Saturday, but federal officials warned that delays and cancellations would continue as airlines worked to reposition aircraft and crews. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said airlines expected to return to full schedules by the end of Sunday. The disruption remained significant Saturday. FlightAware reported more than 6,000 U.S. flight cancellations and over 7,000 delays as of Saturday evening. For some South Florida travelers, those numbers translated into hours spent bouncing between airports and transportation options in hopes of simply getting home.Veterans Karen Matthews and Ron Matthews told WPTV they had been traveling for about 10 hours after their flight from Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport to Baltimore was canceled."Are we ever gonna get home?" Karen Matthews said.Their attempt to find another flight brought them from Fort Lauderdale to Donald J. Trump International Airport, but another cancellation awaited them."To have taken the shuttle bus, the train, the shuttle bus ... and then to get here and it's canceled again," Karen Matthews said.She summed up the experience simply: "This is really frustrating."Ron Matthews said the couple had not had a chance to eat during their lengthy trip."It's been kind of rough," he said. "I've been eating mints all day long just to get by."Ron Matthews said American Airlines reissued their tickets but did not provide them with meals, transportation assistance or other accommodations."No accommodations, just reissuing the tickets," he said. "Nothing, no assistance with transportation, no upgrade of seats or anything, not a thing."For Karen Matthews, reaching home also carried a medical concern. She said she needed to get back to medications she takes for blood pressure and acid reflux."I have to control my blood pressure," she said. "So yes, it's important."The nationwide ground stop began Friday afternoon after a telecommunications failure involving air traffic control infrastructure, federal officials said. The stoppage was lifted shortly after 8 p.m. Friday.Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that a preliminary investigation found the problem occurred while a contractor at a remote FAA facility was replacing aging copper wiring with fiber and working with a router. Officials were still determining whether human error or faulty equipment was responsible.The FAA said airspace was safe and operational Saturday, but airlines still faced the complicated task of getting airplanes, pilots and flight attendants back into position after the nationwide disruption.Another traveler WPTV spoke with, Andrew, said his cancellation came nearly a day after the nationwide disruption."A cancellation the following day, you know, almost 24 hours later, a little bit unexpected," he said.Federal officials said they expected the remaining disruptions to ease through Sunday as airlines rebuilt their schedules. Travelers with upcoming flights should continue checking directly with their airline for the latest status before heading to the airport. For passengers like the Matthews, the nationwide ground stop ending did not mean the travel nightmare was over.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Weeks after historic flooding devastated homes in Jensen Beach, Martin County families are still cleaning up and rebuilding, with volunteers, churches, firefighters, contractors and local leaders joining the recovery effort.Water marks remain visible on some homes, showing how high floodwaters rose. Residents are now removing damaged drywall, clearing debris and collecting donated supplies while seeking financial assistance and answers about the area's drainage systems.Neighbors step in to help Jensen Beach familiesBefore-and-after video from the Jensen Beach neighborhood shows the extent of the flooding, which left several homes under feet of water.Weeks later, homeowner Lisa Marie French said cleaning up has been a major undertaking. We first told you about French's circumstances last week. You first have to empty the houses," French said. "We have to clean the houses; they're filled with mold, we have to take the drywall out."French, whose home was impacted by the flooding, has also helped coordinate community cleanup efforts alongside Christ of Church, Family Church and other organizations. She said neighbors and other volunteers have repeatedly shown up asking what families need and then immediately gotten to work."People have been just coming and just hands-on," French said. "People are like, 'Hey, are you taking donations? What do you need?' And they get out of their cars, and they start working, and that's our neighbors. It’s pretty amazing."Residents seek answers about flooding and drainageAs cleanup continues, residents say they also want answers about what contributed to the severe flooding.Some are questioning how much pumping from Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce into the Savannas Preserve may have contributed to flooding in their neighborhood.Stephen Leighton, chief of staff for U.S. Brian Mast, R-Fla., told WPTV that questions remain as officials work through the recovery process."There's a lot of answers that these residents need, and hopefully we can do that," Leighton said.Leighton also said the state had taken steps toward an emergency declaration and reached out to the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA).Families look for financial assistanceFor some homeowners, rebuilding also brings financial uncertainty.French said her home is not in a flood zone and she does not have flood insurance, leaving her family dependent on whatever assistance, donated materials and volunteer help becomes available."We're trying to get any type of help. We don't have flood insurance here," French said. "We're way above sea level; we are not a flood zone. So it's just whatever volunteers and help and materials we can get is what we get."Community calls for more volunteersResidents say more hands are still needed as families work to make their homes livable again.Leighton said a question-and-answer town meeting with residents and county, state and federal officials is planned this week as the community seeks clarity about the flooding and available assistance.For volunteers, Leighton said even small acts can make a difference for families trying to put their lives back together."To help somebody take that picture off the wall and put it in a box, so they can move on, is a big deal," he said.With Thanksgiving approaching, he said the need for community support remains urgent."We're two weeks out from Thanksgiving, and we really need the community to come together and help," Leighton said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

A nationwide ground stop prompted by air traffic control communications issues caused widespread flight disruptions Friday, with passengers across South Florida facing delays and cancellations.The Federal Aviation Administration said communications issues affecting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers prompted it to ground flights at airports nationwide while technicians investigated. The agency later lifted the ground stop Friday night, though flight disruptions continued.WPTV's Michael Hoffman spent Friday at Donald J Trump International Airport speaking with travelers as departure boards showed numerous delays and cancellations and passengers scrambled to figure out what would happen to their trips. Departure boards showed numerous delays, with some flights being canceled as the disruption continued.One traveler told Hoffman that she and her husband had planned to fly to Atlanta for a weekend trip but were told they likely would not be leaving Friday night."They said it didn't look good," she said, describing what her husband had been told by TSA. "Probably not leaving tonight."Although disappointed, she said their travel wasn't urgent."This (travel to Atlanta) was just for fun, so disappointing," she said. "You know, rather safe than sorry."For some, the disruption came just as they were preparing to leave."I'm about to board the plane, and the pilot stopped everyone and said, 'Hold on, we might have to deplane. Give us a second,'" traveler Hailey Desser said. "And then he's like, 'Yep, everyone needs to get off the plane.'"Sara Haseney appeared to arrive just before operations ground to a halt."I guess we probably were one of the last planes to board or to land, I guess," Haseney said. "But yeah, it was definitely crazy, and I think we're all pretty shocked."For Lindsay Funes, the timing made the disruption particularly stressful."Just kind of annoying, the whole situation, especially like it's my first time traveling on my own and like not with a family member," Funes said.The FAA said the ground stop was ordered after communications issues affected multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers. Technicians began investigating the problem as flights were held on the ground across the countryThe ground stop was issued because of "extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety."Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said officials had no indication at the time that a malicious act or hacking contributed to the communications issues."There is no indication, and we had no reason to believe that as of right now that this was a threat to the United States," said Mullin.Nationwide ground stops are exceptionally rare. The last one occurred in January 2023 after an FAA system outage. Before that, flights were grounded nationwide following the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.The FAA remained in the early stages of investigating the problem, and additional information about what caused the disruption and what was being done to resolve it was not immediately available.At DJT International Airport, the nationwide disruption quickly became personal.Lynne Hernandez told Hoffman her family has a baby shower Saturday morning, but a family member's travel plans were in doubt."She's booked on a flight for tomorrow morning," Hernandez said. "In the event that this ends and she can get on the plane tomorrow morning, we'll see her tomorrow around 11."Hoffman asked her what time the baby shower starts."11," Hernandez responded.For Hernandez's family, even getting on that next flight would leave little room to spare.As the delays and cancellations accumulated, travelers were not only asking when they would get into the air. They also wanted to know what the disruption could mean for their wallets."Is that coming out of my pocket?" Funes asked.Naccarato wondered whether she would be able to scrap the weekend trip altogether and try again later."I would want to know at what point, like, would I be able to get a refund or change my flight for a different weekend?" she said.The FAA lifted the nationwide ground stop at 8:15 p.m. ET Friday after it had been in effect for more than four hours, but airlines continued dealing with delays and cancellations as they worked to reposition aircraft and crews. Travelers with upcoming flights should continue checking directly with their airlines for the status of their individual trips.

For decades, Harry's Banana Farm, a local dive bar, has been hard to miss along Dixie Highway in Lake Worth Beach.There's the raptor on the roof, the colorful atmosphere and the roadside billboard known for its witty, sometimes controversial messages.WATCH REPORT BELOW: "It's iconic; everybody here knows about the place," said Vinnie Fiermonte, who lives in Lake Worth Beach. "A lot of people I know here from Boynton come to Harry's."Tyler Hart, a local who has visited Harry's Banana Farm, said the bar's unusual personality makes it stand out."Definitely the raptor on the roof stands out," Hart said, adding there are "always interesting signs on the billboard."But this week, that billboard is empty as the neighborhood bar mourns the death of its owner, Harry Seifert Jr.Harry died Tuesday from health complications at 76 years old, according to the bar's general manager and Harry's longtime friend, Lou DeStout.DeStout said Harry had survived two strokes over the years and dealt with a number of other health problems.The loss is personal for DeStout, who met Harry in the late 1970s. Their friendship would eventually span decades, other business ventures and Harry's Banana Farm itself."Oh, Harry and I met in the late 70s and, uh, we did a lot, we just hit it off instantly," DeStout said. "And he was a larger-than-life character. We were both notorious wise hats."Harry's connection to the bar went back even further.According to DeStout, Harry's father opened Harry's Banana Farm in 1954. took over in the early 1980s and helped transform it from a more family-oriented establishment into a late-night hangout."Harry's the one that made it that late-night kind of hip place to be because he was like, he was a cool guy," DeStout said.Inside the bar, DeStout said reminders of his longtime friend are everywhere.When WPTV reporter Joel Lopez asked how much of the bar reminded him of Harry, DeStout didn't hesitate."Well, how could, how could it not? The whole place is him," DeStout said."He's the one that decorated all the stuff," he added.DeStout said many of the items inside the bar were collected during Harry's travels, with pieces from places including Australia and China.Inside, the bar's walls are a collage of Harry's travels and adventures with treasures at every inch.Harry was also behind another unmistakable piece of the bar's personality: its roadside sign."He was the original sign guy," DeStout said. "Yeah, way back when he started a tradition."DeStout eventually took over the tradition of putting messages on the sign and said he shared Harry's sense of humor."He always enjoyed it too," DeStout said. "But like I said, he was the original guy who did the sign."Harry's health began declining years ago. DeStout said Harry suffered a stroke roughly 17 years ago that paralyzed one side of his body. He recovered before suffering another stroke that took away his voice."He's had numerous other medical problems over the years, and then he started having heart problems and things like that," DeStout said. "So it's, it's been a difficult bunch of years for him."Still, DeStout said Harry continued living his life, traveling and attending events despite those challenges."He still lived life, and he got around more than I did," DeStout said. "He'd go to Las Vegas to the Sphere and the Kravis Center to plays, and, he got out and about a lot more than I did."Since Harry's death, DeStout said he's repeatedly heard one question from customers and employees: What happens to Harry's Banana Farm now?His answer is simple."Nothing. We're gonna continue on like we always do," DeStout said. "I've had to answer that question 100 times in the last two days. It's gonna keep on being Harry's Banana Farm."DeStout said that longevity is notable as Lake Worth Beach and the surrounding area continue to change. He recalled a time when Harry's was one of several similar neighborhood bars along Dixie Highway."When Harry and I tended bar here together 40 years ago, there was 10 places like Harry's up and down Dixie, and they're all gone," DeStout said. "Harry's is the only one that survives, and not only survives but thrives."For the people closest to Harry, his legacy extends beyond the walls of his neighborhood bar.DeStout said roughly 30 years ago, Harry began dressing as Santa Claus and visiting Barton Elementary School to give wrapped gifts to underprivileged children."He started going to Barton Elementary School and handing out wrapped gifts to all the little kids, underprivileged kids," DeStout said.What started at one school grew to include four elementary schools and eventually became a nonprofit, Harry's Helping Hands."And I just thought when we had the idea of making a legitimate nonprofit, it'd be a great legacy to leave behind," DeStout said. And now, after 30 years, it's gangbusters."The effort is marking its 30th year of giving back to the Lake Worth Beach community."He'd be here for the Christmas party; he'd be proud of everybody here for everything that they've done," DeStout said. "We've come so far, for a little neighborhood bar, we've done quite an impact."For DeStout, giving back is part of the responsibility that comes with operating a successful community business."And I believe, you know, very strongly that when, when you do business in the community, you profit from the community, you have a responsibility and obligation to contribute to that community, you know, so that's, and that was always Harry," DeStout said. "Harry was just so generous."DeStout is now encouraging people who want to honor Harry to donate to Harry's Helping Hands in lieu of flowers."He would much prefer a donation because that goes directly to the kids," DeStout said.Customers have also been stopping by Harry's Banana Farm to remember the man behind the business."He was very sarcastic, funny. He not only gave back, but he was a contributor, an active contributor," said Billy Miller, a patron at Harry's Banana Farm. "I would say he's going to be missed, absolutely."Hart shared a similar sentiment."It's definitely a bummer any time you hear a local person like that passes away, hopefully they're able to keep things going," Hart said.Everything DeStout says suggests that is exactly what they intend to do."This whole place is his legacy," DeStout said.And when Lopez asked what he would say to his longtime friend now, DeStout's answer brought that legacy back to where it started."I'll miss you, pal, but we're just gonna keep rolling along, just like we always have," DeStout said.A celebration of life for Harry Seifert Jr. 6 at the Lake Worth Beach Golf Club.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Somebody's hog has gone rogue, and now Indian River County deputies are trying to bring home the bacon all 250 pounds of it. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office is searching for the owner of a hefty domestic boar hog found in the 5600 block of 69th Street. Weighing an estimated 200 to 250 pounds, the four-legged wanderer is currently being housed safely at the sheriff's office farm while deputies work to track down his owner. See also: Indian River County deputies tussle with alligator displaced by heavy flooding But before anyone can claim the hefty hog, they'll need to prove he's theirs. The sheriff's office is asking anyone who recognizes the animal to contact deputies with a photo or description to verify ownership. For now, the hog is safe and sound at the sheriff's office farm, presumably unaware he's the subject of a countywide search. Anyone who believes the boar belongs to them should contact the Indian River County Sheriff's Office.

A teenager was airlifted to the hospital after a serious crash involving an e-bike and a vehicle in Jensen Beach, per deputies. According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office , the crash happened near the intersection of U.S. 1 and Northwest Goldenrod Road. Deputies and Martin County Fire Rescue crews responded to the scene, where the teenager was flown to St. Mary's Medical Center for treatment. See also: 18-year-old dies after being struck by car in St. Lucie County; family raises concerns The extent of the teen's injuries has not been released. Drivers traveling through the area should expect delays as emergency crews remain on scene. The circumstances surrounding the crash have not been released at this time.

An apparent overturned trailer is causing major traffic delays on Florida's Turnpike in St. Lucie County on Sunday afternoon, with southbound traffic backed up behind the crash. According to Florida 511 , the crash was reported around 12:40 p.m. in the southbound lanes around Mile Marker 165 near Fort Pierce. Traffic camera footage near mile marker 164.9 shows what appears to be a large pink vehicle or trailer overturned across part of the highway, with several vehicles backed up behind it. The right lane is blocked, according to the latest traffic report. See also: Teen seriously injured in Jensen Beach e-bike crash, airlifted to hospital The crash is classified as major, and traffic cameras show congestion stretching four miles behind the crash scene. It is unclear whether anyone was injured or how many vehicles were involved. Drivers traveling southbound through St. Lucie County should expect delays as crews respond to the crash. This is a developing story.

A Russian national pleaded guilty Friday to his role in a Medicare fraud scheme rooted in Palm Beach County, marking the first conviction in a case I first brought to you last year.In federal court, 29-year-old Nika Machutadze, with the help of a translator, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit money laundering. He is one of the defendants linked to a fraudulent medical equipment company in Delray Beach called Sunshine Senior Solutions, and he admitted under oath to his involvement in a money laundering scheme totaling more than $7 million.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Machutadze could face up to 20 years in prison, plus fines, restitution and deportation.Seniors first contacted me last year, sharing Medicare statements for medical equipment they didn't need — or receive — from Sunshine Senior Solutions.While I tallied up hundreds of thousands of dollars in false claims from the statements I reviewed, that was a drop in the bucket, according to federal prosecutors. Federal prosecutors say Sunshine Senior Solutions billed insurers for more than $3 billion, though only a fraction of that was paid out. Machutadze admitted to opening bank accounts for Sunshine Senior Solutions and a second similar business in Texas, and transferring some of the money paid by insurers overseas.I reached out to some of the seniors to share the news of the guilty plea."Oh, that's terrific," said Laura Carmine, of Illinois. "Nice to know that justice can be done.""I'm glad to hear that," said Mike Parrett, of Ohio.I spoke with Machutadze's attorney, Tony Mirvis, after Friday's hearing."The government's evidence was overwhelming," Mirvis said. Mirvis said his client thought he was just taking a job."What I think is important is he's like the tip of the spear," Mirvis said. "I hate to say it, but he's kind of like a victim because the people that got him to work— they're the ones that are making the millions of dollars, and he's making like literally nothing. He's getting in trouble for it."Information filed in Friday's case mentions another defendant, Ibrahim Hilmi, and a second, unnamed co-conspirator. Hilmi, who is also tied to Sunshine Senior Solutions, is scheduled for trial in February."Everybody that's involved with this should get prosecuted, and they should get punished for what they did," Mirvis said.Mirvis told me his client will not be cooperating with federal investigators on any other prosecutions.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Shoppers were out at the South Florida Fairgrounds on Friday looking for bargains at a large resale event featuring children's items. "I love the fact that I can save a lot of money, and I like the shopping experience," said Tatiana, a shopper who drove from Port St. Lucie.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The resale event is run by Just Between Friends Palm Beach, a consignment shop. Among the items for sale were tables of toys, racks of clothing and various accessories from playpens to bicycles and strollers. "Everything here is brought in by local families that have gently used items that their kids have outgrown, and instead of throwing it away, they're able to come bring it here and help other families save on items," says store owner Kim Hazim. Resale shops are growing in popularity as inflation strains family budgets, and Hazim said this event has grown over the years. "We used to be in 15,000 square feet; now we're in 30,000 square feet because that's how many families really need to come out," Hazim said. Many were getting an early jump on holiday shopping with Black Friday coming later this month, but deals are already out there. "Black Friday is almost a month-long event," says money-saving expert Andrea Woroch. "Retailers like Best Buy, Nordstrom, even Sephora, they started rolling out doorbuster-like deals on Nov. 1." She added that good deals are already out there. "If you're seeing a good deal, and again, I think that 30% off benchmark is a great place to make a purchase at," Woroch said. "And keep in mind, some retailers will offer price adjustments within a week or two weeks."

Military Trail reopened Thursday night in both directions near Greenacres after crews completed roadway repairs following the fatal Learjet crash on Nov. 1, according to the Florida Department of Transportation.FDOT said two northbound and two southbound lanes opened to drivers as of 7:05 p.m. Thursday.Crews spent the past 48 hours repairing the roadway, including paving and striping the road. Sidewalk repairs also began Thursday.Earlier Thursday, FDOT said crews had worked overnight and into Thursday morning to reopen the northbound lanes.This area of Military Trail had been closed between 10th Avenue and Forest Hill Boulevard after the Learjet crash created a large crater in the road.The reopening restores traffic in both directions along the affected stretch of Military Trail.Nine people were killed when the Learjet, which departed Austin, Texas, en route to the Bahamas, crashed near Greenacres earlier this month. No one on the ground was seriously injured.

Nearly seven weeks after announcing a statewide voter fraud sweep, Florida's attorney general has released the full list of people charged — and some of the arrests have already raised questions.When Attorney General James Uthmeier announced the sweep on illegal voting in September, just before the midterm elections, his office named 12 of the 20 people charged. After repeated requests, a spokesperson from his office sent investigative reporter Katie LaGrone the full list this week.The 20 defendants span across 13 counties. They include four convicted felons and 16 non-citizens — all of whom, according to the attorney general's office, were ineligible to vote at the time they are accused of casting a ballot.WATCH KATIE LAGRONE'S REPORT BELOW:But over the past few weeks, LaGrone has discovered some of these cases are raising questions.Among them is Astrid Quintana, a lawful permanent resident who had been in the country since she was a toddler and is married to a U.S. Her attorney told us she received a voter ID card before she voted in 2024, believing she could."She had no intention to deceive anybody or to do anything that she believed was illegal," attorney Connor Martin said.In her Quintana's case — and in at least seven other cases involving non-citizens now facing these charges — LaGrone discovered the state citing a law that didn't even exist at the time they were accused of voting.When asked how the state could charge her over a law that didn't exist at the time of her alleged crime, Martin responded, "Well, they cannot."In response to LaGrone's findings, a spokesperson for the attorney general said those investigations are still pending.In Tampa, LaGrone recently caught up with the attorney for Donta White, a convicted felon who is not eligible to vote because he's still on probation for grand theft. The state said the father of two admitted to registering to vote twice and voting early in 2024. According to his attorney, he was also sent a voter ID card."I feel that there's an entrapment issue," attorney Lynley Flagler said. "They want to prosecute voting, but they have not put any checks and balances in place to let people know when they're able to vote and when they can't vote."LaGrone is still reviewing the list of the other defendants charged but of the 20 defendants charged, Duval County has the most with four cases, followed by Hillsborough, with three. The rest are scattered around the state.Here is the full list of 20 defendants charged.Non-citizen voters:Giorgio Mucelli — charges filed in Brevard CountyAstrid Quintana — charges filed in Lee CountyTracey Sabrina Jones — charges filed in Polk CountySelvin Whilby — charges filed in Hillsborough CountyAgnes Donaldson — charges filed in Duval CountyAnthony Powell — charges filed in Hendry CountyKaidan Johnson — charges filed in Lee CountyAllejando Villegas — charges filed in Columbia CountyManon Martine Raux — charges filed in Collier CountyJames Hollingsworth — charges filed in DeSoto CountyCynthia Canales — charges filed in Marion CountyMei-Lin Johnston — charges filed in Okeechobee CountyLerenzo Remolina — charges filed in Hillsborough CountyEdward Doldron — charges filed in Duval CountyRoberto Hernandez — charges filed in Duval CountyCraig Smith — charges filed in Marion CountyFelon voters:Donta White — charges filed in Hillsborough CountyRay Charles Taylor — charges filed in Pinellas CountyWilliam Dietz — charges filed in Duval CountyJivonn Ysbeck — charges filed in Palm Beach County

The Stuart Air Show is preparing to take flight at Witham Field, bringing aircraft, crowds and heavier traffic to the Stuart area.WATCH WPTV'S REPORT:The air show is celebrating its 37th year at Witham Field on Friday and this year's event will feature the F-16 demo team along with a variety of other aircraft. The show runs through Sunday, Nov. 15.WATCH BELOW: What to know about traffic, parking and getting to Witham FieldAmong those participating is Maj. Taylor Hiester, the United States Air Force F-16 Viper Demonstration Team Commander and Pilot stationed at Shaw Air Force Base in Sumter, South Carolina."I've been in the Air Force for 11 years now, and it's been a dream come true for the last three years to serve, not just as a military officer first, but fighter pilot second," Hiester told WPTV Anchor Mike Trim. "To be the American fighter pilot that gets to connect the American people with the people that do their business around the world on their behalf, is very special."The 37th annual air show features F-16s, large military planes, ghost riders, aerobatic planes and skydivers, along with games and food for families."It's for me, my last performance and for a lot of performers, it's that it's the close out of the year," Hiester told WPTV. "So, it is a wonderful cocktail of emotions that come together that make a fantastic show for the people of Florida, and I think that the people are going to notice that there's something special."Beyond the flight demonstrations, the event also focused on education and STEM classesWPTV First Alert Weather Meteorologist Kate Wentzel spoke with students from the aerospace club from Jupiter Christian, along with students from the Parker area, the Virginia Beach area, Fort Pierce and around the Treasure Coast. "In the air show, they want to partner with all of these school groups and organizations, because really it empowers them and inspires them to go into aviation-related careers," Wentzel said.Weather plays a critical role in aviation, and the students learned how it affects pilots."We talked about winds, how that impacts pilots. Pilots want to take off into the wind, because the wind blowing over the wings, gives them better lift and a faster lift speed," Wentzel said. "They also want to land into the wind, because if they have a tailwind pushing them too strong, it can make it difficult for the pilot to have a controlled landing."Students also learned how icing can impact aircraft at high altitudes and near thunderstorms. Aircraft are supposed to stay 20 miles away from severe thunderstorms at all times, because that is where big updrafts and gusty winds develop, Wentzel said.Conditions are expected to be clear and breezy this evening, making for good viewing of the Stuart Air Show.

A Wellington man has been sentenced to seven years in federal prison for a fraud scheme that prosecutors say used fake cosmetic surgery clinics and the stolen identities of more than 100 people to obtain millions of dollars from medical lenders.Jacquez Dion Tullis, 42, was sentenced Thursday to 84 months in prison after previously pleading guilty to conspiracy to commit bank fraud and aggravated identity theft, according to the U.S. Department of Justice.U.S. Ruiz II sentenced Tullis to 60 months for the bank fraud conspiracy charge and a consecutive 24 months for aggravated identity theft.Tullis was also ordered to serve five years of supervised release and pay more than $2.3 million in restitution. The court also ordered a forfeiture money judgment of more than $2.3 million.According to court documents and Tullis' admissions in his plea, Tullis and his co-conspirators created six sham medical clinics between April 2018 and February 2024.The clinics purported to provide cosmetic surgery and other medical services but provided no actual care, prosecutors said.The conspirators registered the clinics with the Florida Department of State using stolen personal information belonging to practicing doctors and other people without their knowledge or consent, according to the Justice Department.Prosecutors said some doctors were falsely identified as clinic owners in applications seeking approval as merchants with medical lenders.Once the clinics were approved, the conspirators submitted fraudulent credit applications in the names of more than 100 people. The applications sought approximately $3.1 million and falsely claimed the money would pay for cosmetic surgery and other medical services.The people whose identities were used did not authorize the applications or receive treatment, prosecutors said. According to the Justice Department, death records showed some of the purported patients had died before the dates they supposedly received medical care.The scheme ultimately defrauded medical lenders of approximately $2.3 million, according to prosecutors.Federal prosecutors said Tullis was also involved in a separate scheme targeting a pandemic-era federal relief program.Between April and August 2020, Tullis submitted at least nine fraudulent applications to the U.S. Small Business Administration's Economic Injury Disaster Loan program, according to the Justice Department.The applications sought a combined $696,860 and included false information about businesses' numbers of employees and revenue, prosecutors said.Tullis pleaded guilty July 21 to conspiracy to commit bank fraud and aggravated identity theft.Two co-defendants were previously sentenced in connection with the case.Taneika Nakia Pace, 50, of Hallandale Beach, who prosecutors said managed two of the sham clinics, was sentenced in September to six months in prison after pleading guilty to bank fraud.Junaque Nicole Tullis, 46, of Coral Springs, was sentenced in August to eight months in prison after pleading guilty to wire fraud in connection with fraudulent Economic Injury Disaster Loan applications.All three defendants were charged as part of the Justice Department's 2025 National Health Care Fraud Takedown.The FBI investigated the case.

The northbound lanes of Florida's Turnpike are closed in Palm City following a crash involving a tractor-trailer and a pickup truck Friday morning.The crash happened just before 11 a.m. near mile marker 137, according to Martin County Fire Rescue.Officials said both drivers are safe and no injuries have been reported.Martin County Fire Rescue, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office and Florida Highway Patrol are working to clear debris from the roadway.Drivers are being asked to avoid the area, seek alternate routes and expect delays.It was not immediately clear when the northbound lanes would reopen.

Interstate 95 in Indian River County was shut down in both directions early Friday morning, creating a major traffic disruption for drivers near the Indian River-St. Lucie County line.WATCH: Lt. Indiana Miranda gives update after man dies in trooper-involved shooting incidentOn Thursday, at about 11:20 p.m., FHP said a trooper was involved in a shooting incident on I-95 near mile marker 141. According to FHP, the incident began when the trooper initiated a traffic stop for a man driving over 90 mph near mile marker 138. Another trooper joined as back up and that's when, FHP said, the man got aggressive and was uncooperative. "The primary trooper who completed the stop addressed the driver and advised him the reason for the stop was the speed, asked him for his driver's license and registration, he noticed that the driver was hostile," Lt. Indiana Miranda said during a press conference on Friday. "There was a little bit of back and forth between the two, at which point the driver says, 'I don't want to talk to you,' and there was cursing by the driver to our primary trooper."The second trooper stepped in, asking for the man's driver's license as well. That is when the man accelerated and fled the traffic stop, resulting in a pursuit. The pursuit escalated, when the suspect fired a gun at troopers, with one of the troopers returning fire."He said over the radio that there were shots being fired at them. Our trooper returned fire, while driving his vehicle and he was able to engage in a PIT," Miranda said.FHP said the officers used a PIT maneuver causing the suspect to crash and rollover. Authorities said no troopers were injured during the shooting. The suspect was pronounced dead at the scene. FHP initially said the suspect sustained injuries from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound. However, during the 2 p.m. press conference, FHP said that it is not clear who fired the shot that killed the suspect and that is under investigation.FHP said the Florida Department of Law Enforcement is investigating and the two FHP troopers are currently on paid administrative leave pending the outcome of the investigation.All northbound and southbound lanes of I-95 were closed for several hours into the morning. All lanes have since reopened.

The Stuart Air Show is preparing to take flight at Witham Field, bringing aircraft, crowds and heavier traffic to the Stuart area.The air show is celebrating its 37th year at Witham Field. Lee Potter with the Stuart Air Show said this year's event will feature the F-16 demo team along with a variety of other aircraft arriving throughout the week.For drivers, planning the route before leaving home can help make the trip easier.Drivers coming from Interstate 95 can take the Stuart exit and use Kanner Highway to Monterey Road.Drivers using Florida's Turnpike can take Southwest Martin Downs Boulevard. 1 and Dixie Highway are also options for reaching Monterey Road.As drivers approach Witham Field, they should follow posted signs and directions from law enforcement.The air show has two drive-in entrances off Monterey Road, with the Martin County Sheriff's Office directing traffic in the area.General parking is free in designated Stuart Air Show parking areas.Complimentary shuttle service will take visitors from the parking areas to the main gates. ADA parking is also available.Drivers should not create their own parking spots or park outside the designated areas.The best advice: stick with the official parking lots, watch for posted signs and follow law enforcement directions as you approach the air show.WPTV Traffic Reporter Johann Hoffend will be at Witham Field with traffic and transportation information for people heading to the Stuart Air Show.

From high-water rescues to the heroes who live next door, people are sharing their stories about the good Samaritans who came to their aid during the recent floods that ravaged our area.Tessie Watts from Riviera Beach says first responders and the mayor of her city pulled her to safety after she fled her home and more than 20 inches of water.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Nicole Vazquez from Fort Pierce shared with WPTV anchor Hollani Davis that her brother is her hero. She said he helped the family sandbag their home before leaving, then came back by boat to get them out."He left, and he came back Tuesday to evacuate us, and then we took shelter with him that night," says Vazquez.The selfless acts stretched to West Palm Beach, where Miles Bradford and his friend jumped in to help stranded drivers."If it was me, I would want someone to get out there and help me," says Bradford.Long after the water is gone, even though there will undoubtedly be more tough days ahead, it's these acts of kindness that people say they'll remember.

Lucie is getting closer to welcoming its first professional soccer team, with a groundbreaking ceremony for a new 6,000-seat stadium scheduled for Saturday, Dec. Lucie Sports Club announced Thursday that construction will begin at Walton & One, where the stadium will sit on approximately six acres.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The club is preparing to compete in USL League One in 2027, and the new stadium is expected to serve as more than just a place to watch soccer. Plans call for a year-round destination where families and community members can gather for entertainment and other events.The development group will fully fund construction of the stadium and has entered into an agreement with the City of Port St. Lucie to use the land."From day one, we knew this had to be about much more than building a soccer club," said Gustavo Suárez, founder and CEO of Port St. "We set out to create something that feels like a true part of this community, a place where families can gather, young players can dream, and new traditions can take shape."The groundbreaking ceremony will begin at noon on Dec. 12, bringing together club leaders, USL representatives, partners and founding members.A public celebration will follow at 1:30 p.m., featuring food trucks, entertainment and activities for all ages.The club says more details about the event will be announced in the coming weeks.

What was once a sprawling cattle pasture in western Martin County now looks more like a lake.What residents described as 3 to 4 feet of floodwater currently covers parts of Hungryland Farms in the Trailside community, forcing cattle to wade and swim through submerged pastures in search of dry ground.WATCH REPORT BELOW: But for the families who live and work there, the flooding is more than a natural disaster. They say it's a crisis years in the making — one they warned officials about as far back as 2018.Documents obtained by WPTV show residents raised concerns about drainage problems long before last week's historic rainfall inundated the Treasure Coast.Now, with the rain gone but the water lingering, residents are questioning whether the devastation could have been prevented.Melissa, who raises grass-fed cattle at Hungryland Farms in the rural Trailside community, says the flooding has transformed her property almost overnight."It feels like Lake Okeechobee," she said.Her cattle, accustomed to grazing freely across the farm, are now navigating deep floodwater. "It's completely covered," Melissa said. they're all underwater."The flooding has left her animals without their primary food source and exposed them to potentially deadly hazards, including drowning, waterborne parasites and electrical dangers.Melissa pointed to an electrical transformer nearly submerged by floodwater, questioning whether her cattle could be electrocuted if they wandered too close.And despite the rain stopping, she said the water isn't draining — it's rising. "We always thought we were through because the rain had stopped, but the water kept rising," she said.For Trailside Homeowners Association President Kyla Shay, the flooding is the culmination of years of unresolved drainage concerns.In a 2018 letter obtained by WPTV, Shay warned homeowners that property south of Trailside had effectively become a reservoir, with water rising as much as 3.5 feet above community roads and breaching a berm — a raised barrier designed to control water flow.That same year, Shay contacted the South Florida Water Management District, warning that blocked drainage had left some pastures under 8 feet of water.She asked for help but says the underlying problems were never resolved."It's a combination of years of 'We'll get to it,' and we never got to it," Shay said.Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton acknowledges the community faces significant drainage challenges.Gorton said a berm breached Monday on the county-owned Elise J Property northeast of Trailside, sending water into a nearby canal, with some water backflowing into the community."We still can't get back to that breach," Gorton told investigative reporter Kate Hussey, explaining that high water levels have prevented crews from accessing the area.But the larger problem, he said, is Trailside's geography.The community is essentially a bathtub, surrounded by berms, hundreds of acres of wetlands and two independent water control districts.Water flows into the area, but there is only one drainage ditch for it to slowly escape."There's no easy way to get that water out except by pump or gravity," Gorton said.WPTV contacted engineer Bob Higgins, who works with both the Pal Mar Water Control District and the Hobe St. Lucie Conservancy District.Higgins said a potential solution had already been designed years ago: an outfall that would allow water to drain through the R G Mitigation Bank Preserve to the south and the neighboring Elise J property, which Martin County acquired in 2026. But that project was never built.When Hussey asked Gorton whether the county had been aware of the proposal, he confirmed officials had discussed it with the property's former owner."We did have some dialogue with the previous owner of Elise J about creating a formal water control structure that could discharge before the berms would breach," Gorton said.According to Gorton, the former owners submitted two permit applications to the South Florida Water Management District, but construction never began.WPTV contacted the former property owners, who said they did not know why the project was never completed.When Hussey reached out to the South Florida Water Management District, the agency said Trailside was outside its jurisdiction.However, Gorton said the district had permitted every property within Trailside and oversaw the proposed drainage project.Hussey followed up with the district, seeking clarification about its jurisdiction and asking why the drainage project was never constructed.The district has not responded to those follow-up questions.Despite the years of delays, Gorton said there may finally be a path forward."The good news is the county purchased that property, and it's our intent to bring that project forward," he said.Gorton said he has already requested the original permit applications in hopes of expediting approval — and construction— of the project.He also plans to return Friday to assess the flooding and determine what immediate relief may be possible."We're looking at ways to get the water out faster," he said.But for residents like Melissa, every additional day underwater carries a cost. "This could be a very costly natural disaster for us," she said.Her cattle still need to eat. Their pastures are submerged. And with no clear timeline for when the water will recede, the future of her farm remains uncertain."I don't have any food," Melissa said to her cows. "I'm sorry."For now, Hungryland Farms is living up to its name — and the families who depend on it are waiting for the water to go down.WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey continues to seek answers from the South Florida Water Management District about the proposed drainage project and why it was never completed.

Playing sports can get expensive, especially when you have to pay for all the gear. But one high school student is finding a creative way to combine her favorite sport and giving back. Ella Axtell is a senior at The Benjamin School and founded "Gear for Goals."WATCH: High school senior scores big by giving soccer gear to kids in need"Gear for Goals is an organization that I go and take used and new soccer gear and equipment, and I take it to kids who are less fortunate," Axtell said.Axtell donates the soccer gear to centers like Place of Hope, Family First and Quantum House."They come in there using their wheelchairs. We play soccer with them in any way that they are. We equip them, and it's crazy, they love it so much. They always say how it's able to give them a place to play and give them an advantage to play," Axtell said.She also hosts clinics to teach kids how to play."I love it. I honestly love it because I really do think every kid should have the chance to play, and I don't want one kid not to be able to if they don't have the gear," Axtell said.Gear for Goals is not only helping young athletes in Palm Beach County, but across the world."We've gone all over. I went to Costa Rica internationally with St. Mark's and I held four days in that week. I held soccer clinics and each kid got a full entire kit from shirts to cleats," Axtell said.Axtell said when she came up with the idea for “Gear for Goals”, she started posting online.“We have an Instagram called @Gear_for_goals, and I send out flyers and post all the time about it. And then I started reaching out to other places that I could have boxes at. So I had one at Palm Beach Gardens Rec Center,” Axtell said. “I actually was able to host a soccer drive for dressing for charity at St. Mark's, and we raised money, and got a bunch of money for that. And I just spread the word, have an Amazon wish list. I'm just emailing, emailing, emailing.”Donations have flooded in, with people giving new and slightly used soccer gear or buying from her online equipment wishlist."I just want to continue it. I want to continue it through college. I want to keep going, see how big we can grow and hopefully one day we'll be so big that we'll have clinics all over the world," Axtell said.While helping kids score goals, Axtell says her goal is to grow the organization. She says they're always looking for donations and volunteers. To donate or learn more, visit the @Gear_for_Goals Instagram page.

The Indianapolis Colts got the respite they needed.After losing five straight and enduring three weeks of tumult, they finally celebrated a victory.Daniel Jones threw for one score, Seth McGowan ran for another and Adetomiwa Adebawore recovered a fumble for a touchdown on Sunday as the Colts held on for a 24-22 victory over the Miami Dolphins to end their skid."It definitely feels good to win," Jones said. "It's hard to win in the NFL, so you have to enjoy them."Colts fans didn't seem to enjoy this one much.Some showed up wearing bags over their heads after Indy shipped away two Pro Bowl captains and their top two receivers before the trade deadline. The Colts held onto Jones and star running back Jonathan Taylor, who said goodbye to Indy fans last week only to suit up again and finish with 103 total yards.While he helped the Colts (3-7) rush for 172 yards, Jones was booed loudly during the second half, when he had just one completion beyond the line of scrimmage. Jones was 11 of 22 for 108 yards with two interceptions.Indy was also flagged 13 times, several of which prevented the Colts from sealing the victory sooner. They wound up needing a fourth-down stop with 1:36 left and McGowan's run for a first down on the ensuing possession to close it out.The offense's struggles led to questions about a possible quarterback switch, which coach Shane Steichen quickly shut down because Indy plays Thursday night."Yeah, he'll be the starting quarterback this week," Steichen said of Jones. "I think we need to continue to get better. There are a lot of things that happen out there every day, self-inflicted wounds for sure, but we've all got to be better."Kyle McCord had a solid starting debut for Miami (1-8), which lost its third straight. He was 17 of 32 for 209 yards, ran for a score and lost one fumble in place of Malik Willis, who went on injured reserve earlier this week with a groin injury. Ollie Gordon II had 20 carries for 76 yards.Miami missed three kicks, including a 51-yard field goal attempt in the fourth quarter that would have given the Dolphins the lead."We've got to make the extra point, and we've got to make the field goal," coach Jeff Hafley said. "It's 24-22, we miss an extra point, which forces us to go for 2, and we miss two field goals, that's seven points. We have to make those."Indy broke a 7-7 tie when Jones found Laquon Treadwell for a 7-yard TD with 39 seconds left in the first half. It was Treadwell's first TD catch since 2021 with Jacksonville.The Colts then swung the game on the Dolphins' first play of the second half when cornerback Justin Walley stripped McCord near the Miami goal line and Adebawore fell on the ball in the end zone to make it 21-7.Zane Gonzalez made a 53-yard field goal to cut the Dolphins' deficit to 21-10, and Miami got within 21-16 on Chris Johnson's 59-yard interception return for a TD — ending the Dolphins' 46-game stretch without a pick-6 that dated to 2023.Shane Spencer extended Indy's margin to 24-16 with a 51-yard field goal, and McCord scored on a 3-yard run before his 2-point conversion pass was broken up by A.J. Haulcy to keep the Colts ahead by two.Dolphins: Miami played without C Aaron Brewer (concussion protocol) and lost DT Zeek Biggers (knee) in the first half. Backup C Andrew Meyer left late in the game with a stinger but returned.Colts: Indy's offensive line already was short-handed without RT Jalen Travis (knee) and it got thinner when LT Bernhard Raimann entered the concussion protocol in the first quarter. The Colts' bigger concern may be the secondary, which lost All-Pro CB Sauce Gardner (calf) and Pro Bowl CB Charvarius Ward (leg) in the third quarter.Gonzalez was wide left on field goal tries from 47 and 51 yards, and the second would have given the Dolphins the lead. He also missed the extra point after the interception return. Gonzalez was promoted from the practice squad Friday after making 5 of 7 field goals and all five of his extra point attempts over the previous three games.Taylor nearly became the fifth Colts player to reach 10,000 yards from scrimmage. He needed 104 yards to join Hall of Famers Marvin Harrison, Edgerrin James and Lenny Moore and current receivers coach Reggie Wayne. But he finished with 16 carries for 83 yards and two catches for 20 yards, leaving him with 9,999.Dolphins: At Buffalo next Sunday.Colts: Go for a season sweep when they visit Houston on Thursday.

Italian food, live music and family traditions return to Abacoa Town Center this weekend as the Galbani Feast of Little Italy celebrates its 25th anniversary Nov. 6-8 with three days of festivities and free admission, according to organizers.The festival runs from 4 to 10 p.m. Sunday.This year's milestone celebration includes Italian food, cooking demonstrations, live entertainment, family activities and an unusual attempt to make festival history using string cheese.Food is at the heart of the weekend.Festival organizers say guests can expect Italian-American favorites including pasta, sausage and peppers, Neapolitan pizza, zeppole, cannoli and gelato.The Galbani Cooking Stage will feature demonstrations throughout the weekend, giving festivalgoers a chance to watch chefs prepare dishes and pick up cooking tips.The published lineup includes Anthony Acampa, Sicilian Oven Chef Andrew, Galbani Chef Marco Sciortino (with special guest Joe Gannascoli from The Sopranos), Cooking with Vinny, Nina's Fresh Bakery and Michelin-starred chef Joe Isidori. Voga wine seminars are also scheduled during the weekend.Saturday brings one of the festival's most unusual attractions.At 4 p.m., organizers are inviting festivalgoers to participate in an event billed as “Let's Make Italian Festival History!” The goal is to bring people together to simultaneously string string cheese.The public is encouraged to participate, turning a familiar snack into one of the quirkiest moments of the festival's 25th anniversary.The 25th anniversary celebration also brings three days of live entertainment to Abacoa.Friday's schedule includes Angelo Venuto before The Studio 54 Band takes the main stage at 8 p.m.Saturday's lineup includes Daniela Martino at 3 p.m., with Frank Stallone headlining at 8 p.m.Sunday's performers include James Valenti and Franco Corso. The weekend also features DJs, dance performances and additional musical acts.The weekend is about more than food and entertainment.Little Smiles is kicking off its holiday toy drive at the festival. The nonprofit is asking guests to stop by its tent with a new, unwrapped toy to help children in need.Families will also find activities for children throughout the festival, adding another option for parents looking for something to do together in Jupiter this weekend.The combination of a free community festival, a milestone anniversary and opportunities to give back gives Palm Beach County families a timely way to spend the weekend while celebrating a tradition that has grown over 25 years.The Galbani Feast of Little Italy takes place Nov. 6-8 at Abacoa Town Center in Jupiter.Friday: 4-10 p.m.Saturday: 11 a.m.-10 p.m.Sunday: 11 a.m.-7 p.m.General admission is free. Organizers also offer separately priced VIP experiences.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. If you've ever admired a perfectly golden Thanksgiving turkey and wondered how professional chefs make it look so good, Okeechobee Steakhouse co-owner Ralph Lewis has a surprisingly simple answer."It's butter."And not just a little butter.During a recent Thanksgiving cooking demonstration at Okeechobee Prime Meat Market, Lewis stood beside a giant inflatable stick of butter, worked from a table piled high with butter and seasonings, and even pulled a backup rubber stick of butter from his pocket.For Lewis, butter isn't simply an ingredient. It's the foundation of a great Thanksgiving turkey."Are you really supposed to have a budget with butter?" Lewis joked. "Those two words do not go together."According to Lewis, the biggest mistake many home cooks make is putting all of their butter on the outside of the bird.Instead, he recommends carefully separating the skin from the breast meat and creating pockets beneath the skin.Once those pockets are created, it's time to start adding butter.Lots of butter."You just want to keep working it in there," Lewis said. That's impossible, literally impossible, and that's a chef's code."As the turkey cooks, the butter melts beneath the skin, helping keep the meat moist while contributing to the rich color and flavor many Thanksgiving hosts are trying to achieve.After working butter beneath the skin, Lewis also coats the outside of the turkey before adding seasoning.One of the most useful tips Lewis shared involves seasoning the butter before it ever touches the bird.Start by taking butter out of the refrigerator and allowing it to soften to room temperature.Then combine the softened butter with herbs and seasonings such as:Kosher saltFreshly ground black pepperThymeRosemarySageMix everything together until it forms a seasoned compound butter.Then spread that butter beneath the skin and across the exterior of the turkey.By combining the herbs and seasoning directly into the butter, the flavors are distributed more evenly throughout the turkey as it cooks.Lewis says it's a simple step that can make a noticeable difference in flavor.Allow butter to come to room temperature.Mix the butter with kosher salt, black pepper, thyme, rosemary, sage or your favorite herbs.Gently separate the skin from the breast meat without tearing it.Spread seasoned butter beneath the skin and continue working it throughout the breast area.Coat the exterior of the turkey with additional butter.Add additional herbs and seasoning as desired.Place about a half-inch to one inch of water, chicken stock or turkey stock in the bottom of the pan.Cover the turkey with foil and roast at approximately 325 degrees.About 30 minutes before the turkey is done, remove the foil and increase the heat.Lewis says this final step helps create the deep golden-brown color that makes a Thanksgiving turkey look picture-perfect.Of course, Lewis' demonstration included a healthy helping of humor.At one point, while explaining his butter-heavy technique, he declared there is no such thing as too much butter.When told that Thanksgiving calories don't count, he quickly fired back:"What's calories?"And when asked whether anything should go inside the turkey cavity itself, his answer was immediate."Well, butter, of course."For families looking to spend less time in the kitchen and more time around the dinner table, Okeechobee Prime Meat Market is offering a variety of Thanksgiving meal packages featuring roasted or smoked turkeys, prime rib, beef tenderloin, traditional sides and holiday desserts.The market's Ultimate Holiday Family Feast serves 16 to 18 people and includes a Bell & Evans all-natural turkey, prime roasted beef tenderloin, stuffing, mashed potatoes, gravy, cranberry sauce and more.Pre-orders are available through Okeechobee Prime Meat Market in West Palm Beach.This article was drafted with the assistance of Microsoft Copilot using reporting, interview transcripts, and information gathered by WPTV journalist T.A. All facts, quotes, and editorial decisions were reviewed by WPTV before publication.What do you want me to Shine A Light on? What are you most proud of where you live? Email me at tawalker@wptv.com.

Palm Beach County residents can take one Thanksgiving task off their list while helping feed a neighbor in need through Pie It Forward, a fundraiser benefiting Meals on Wheels of the Palm Beaches.Meals on Wheels Special Events Director Maura Sartory said local chefs from restaurants and country clubs donate pies that are sold through the campaign. Proceeds from each pie sold help feed a senior for one week.WATCH REPORT BELOW: "We sell them online now through Nov. 18, and each pie we sell is available for pickup that Tuesday of Thanksgiving week," Sartory said. "You get a pie and the proceeds feed a senior for a week."The campaign includes traditional Thanksgiving favorites such as pumpkin, pecan and apple pies, along with key lime pies.Orders are available through Nov. 18, although organizers say pies can sell out before the deadline.A pie without the piePeople who will be traveling for Thanksgiving or simply don't need another dessert can still participate.Sartory said Pie It Forward offers a virtual pie, which allows people to make a donation without receiving a physical pie."A lot of people travel during the holidays, so they can still support," Sartory said. "We have a way they can buy a virtual pie, which is simply a donation. No physical pie is received, and you feed a senior for a week."And there is one additional benefit to the virtual version.When WPTV's T.A. Walker asked Sartory how many calories were in a virtual pie, her answer was simple: "Zero."Students and Girl Scouts pitch inThe community effort extends beyond the chefs making the pies.Students from the Palm Beach School for Autism help assemble the boxes used for the fundraiser."Our students train in a number of Duffy's restaurants, and we're helping Meals on Wheels, kind of putting the boxes together and just helping this great cause," Patrick Pierre Jr. said.Girl Scouts are also lending a hand by decorating boxes with Thanksgiving messages for the people who receive them.Melinda Glasco of Girl Scouts of Southeast Florida said the project is a natural fit with the organization's mission."Part of the Girl Scout mission is making the world a better place, and this is a great way to partner with some amazing organizations and do just that," Glasco said.The Girl Scouts earn a special Meals on Wheels patch for participating in the assembly.Duffy's continues a community traditionDuffy's Sports Grill is contributing 300 pies to the effort this year and has supported Pie It Forward since its early years.Geri Emmett said the Duffy's Foundation's participation also carries personal meaning because of her late husband, Paul Emmett."He was always community-minded," Emmett said. "My late husband, Paul Emmett, and Duffy's has followed in those footsteps all the way along."For families still planning their Thanksgiving meal, the approaching Nov. 18 ordering deadline creates a chance to accomplish two things at once: bring home dessert and help Meals on Wheels serve a Palm Beach County neighbor.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. "So this is our nonprofit organization, and we put together an adult special needs cheer team."The team's first high school football appearance is scheduled for Oct. 22 at Palm Beach Lakes High School.Scott said the goal was to create an opportunity without barriers, allowing participants to experience the excitement, teamwork and recognition that come with being part of a cheer squad."We wanted to give everyone an opportunity to have literally no limits on being able to cheer and feel inclusive and feel important," Scott said.During a recent practice, members of the team performed one of their cheers and shared what the program means to them.For participant Sheila, the experience goes far beyond learning routines."I love it here at Passionate Care," Sheila said. Many businesses are reeling in the effects of last week’s historic flooding event across South Florida, including a local Vero Beach citrus grove farm. CBS12 News Photojournalist Chris Pollock visited Greene Sugars Farm in Vero Beach, a family-owned farm business that spans multiple generations. The farm has been amongst the hardest hit from the historic flooding. Aubrey Greene shared with CBS12 News that they had a great citrus season last year, and were anticipating another good year this year, that was until the flooding put their crops, trees, and livestock in jeopardy. Greene Sugars boasts 800 acres of lemon trees, 50 acres of sugar belle trees, and 1000’s of cattle. They put out roughly 60,000-80,000 boxes of citrus per year and have a contract with Coca-Cola. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium Greene shared that the farm was hit with over 10 inches of rain in one single night, and that the citrus groves have been flooded trunk to trunk in water for over a week, despite heavy pumping every morning and night. That amount of rain over all of this land, it’s crazy, Greene said.

Veterans of all eras and residents of all ages packed Veterans Memorial Park in Port St. Lucie on Wednesday for the annual Veterans Day ceremony.WPTV anchor and Navy veteran Mike Trim connected with fellow veterans about the significance of the day.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Vietnam veteran Michael Greene wore a newly decorated vest commemorating his Army service "It's all like my whole history. Learning to navigate without relying on sight requires skills many people may never have considered, from using a white cane to technology that reads or magnifies what's on a computer screen.At Lighthouse for the Blind of the Palm Beaches, Treasure Coast & Okeechobee in West Palm Beach, those tools are helping people who are blind or visually impaired build greater independence.The organization serves people ranging from babies to seniors across five counties, executive director Lisa Stella told WPTV.For children, that can include activities designed to be sensory-oriented and inclusive in the community.One of the skills taught at the Lighthouse is how to use a white cane to navigate an environment.During WPTV's visit, Shining A Light reporter T.A. Walker put on a blindfold and attempted a mobility exercise with Elizabeth Prus, Lighthouse for the Blind's youth services director.Prus instructed Walker to sweep the cane back and forth roughly the width of his shoulders as he walked. The cane provided information about objects in his path, including a chair and a kitchen island."This is a tool that people who are visually impaired use to navigate environments," Prus said.The training can begin at a young age."We start with little kids, teaching them how to use a cane so that way they can travel independently," Prus said.For Walker, temporarily navigating without sight offered a firsthand look at how a white cane can provide information about the environment around him.The Lighthouse also helps clients use technology designed to make computers more accessible to people who are blind or have low vision.Brandon Butzberger demonstrated ZoomText Fusion, software he uses on a computer."It's called ZoomText Fusion," Butzberger said. "It's a software that has the screen reading (narration) capabilities that Tekesha is showing, as well as magnification."Tekesha Saffold also demonstrated audio software she uses to navigate her computer.Both Butzberger and Saffold are former Lighthouse clients who later became employees, turning their own experiences with the organization into an opportunity to help others.That full-circle journey provides another example of what independence can look like.Butzberger is now an adjustment to blindness counselor at the Lighthouse, while Saffold works as an intake specialist.Their experiences show how skills and resources designed to increase independence can carry beyond a classroom or training session and into education, employment and everyday life.The Lighthouse's work spans generations. Stella said the organization serves people from babies through seniors across Palm Beach, Martin, St. Lucie, Indian River and Okeechobee counties.Mobility training is one piece of that work. Assistive technology provides another.Together, the demonstrations at the West Palm Beach Lighthouse offered a look at how people who are blind or visually impaired can use training, technology and practical tools to navigate their surroundings and perform everyday tasks independently.For some former clients, the journey has come full circle. After receiving services themselves, they're now working at the Lighthouse and helping others develop skills of their own.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI.
